text: Meridian Health Partners is a mid-size healthcare network with three clinics, a legacy on-prem patient record system called MediCore, a newer analytics platform in AWS, a hybrid workforce, and a billing vendor with standing access into its systems. This lesson designs a zero trust architecture for all of it at once, across four domains: identity, micro-segmentation, assume-breach containment, and data and application controls.

Step one and two make Entra ID the single policy decision point, syncing on-prem Active Directory in with Kerberos armoring so every sign-in, on-prem or cloud, runs through one policy engine instead of two. The Conditional Access policy shown here checks sign-in risk level and device compliance together, with continuous access evaluation enabled, so a session can be re-checked mid-stream, not just once at login.

Step three and four replace Meridian's flat on-prem network with four named segments: Clinical Systems, Corporate IT, Partner/Vendor, and Guest/BYOD. No segment reaches Clinical Systems or Partner/Vendor directly anymore. A software-defined perimeter broker evaluates identity and device signals on every request to MediCore, replacing a VPN tunnel that used to grant broad reachability for an entire session.

Step five and six design for the breach that gets through anyway. Lateral movement controls block workstation-to-workstation protocols like SMB and RDP across segment boundaries entirely, so a compromised Corporate IT laptop has no network path into Clinical Systems. The containment playbook shown here detects an impossible-travel, high-risk sign-in, automatically revokes sessions and forces re-authentication, then quarantines the device only if it touched a sensitive segment -- an automated last line of defense, not the first response to every anomaly.

Step seven and eight classify what actually matters -- patient health information in MediCore and the analytics platform -- and wrap MediCore behind an API gateway. Every service-to-service call, including the AWS analytics platform and the ClaimFlow billing vendor, authenticates with a short-lived workload identity token instead of a static shared secret. Notice the vendor's token is scoped to exactly one action, claims:submit, and expires in fifteen minutes -- a design decision this chapter's case study comes back to directly.

This lesson built the architecture across identity, segmentation, containment, and data controls as one coherent design instead of four separate topics. Lesson 30 takes this same design and scores it against the CISA Zero Trust Maturity Model's five pillars, then turns the gaps that scoring reveals into a phased, multi-year rollout roadmap.
